title: Token-Based Authentication
learning_outcomes: Explain how token-based authentication affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from access tokens and refresh tokens to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on token-based authentication in authentication, authorization, and identity. You will connect access tokens and refresh tokens to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Token-Based Authentication matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying access tokens and refresh tokens deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 115 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 115: Access tokens and refresh tokens → Bearer-token requests → Token expiration and renewal → Secure token storage and transmission.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A credential may identify a caller; policy checks decide whether that caller can perform this operation on this resource. In this lesson, treat “Token-Based Authentication” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Token-Based Authentication
content_blocks.code:
GET /v1/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.test
Authorization: Bearer <short-lived-access-token>
Accept: application/json

# The server validates token signature/issuer/audience/expiry,
# then checks the caller's permission for this specific resource.
content_blocks.expected_output: A valid token authenticates a caller but does not automatically authorize every action or resource.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Access tokens and refresh tokens”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Bearer-token requests” and “Secure token storage and transmission”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Authentication establishes identity; authorization must still check the requested action and resource. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating token-based authentication. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.

content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Token-Based Authentication with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating token-based authentication as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
